explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Moses, Israel's leader, says it plain: “At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts.” Seven years go by, and the lender lets go of what his neighbor owes him. A creditor in that land had a standing appointment to let things go.

I understand the guess, because collecting is what a creditor normally does. But verse 2 turns that around: “He is not to collect anything from his neighbor or brother…” So when the seven years end, the lender doesn't collect. He cancels what he loaned, and the debt is gone, not just put on hold.

Picture a lender with a neat little ledger, writing everything down in his best handwriting. The text never mentions record keeping. It says the creditor must cancel what he loaned to his neighbor. All that careful ink gets set aside when the seventh year rolls around.

explanations.answer: The LORD's time of release has been proclaimed
explanations.explanation: That's the reason in verse 2: “…because the LORD’s time of release has been proclaimed.” No loophole, no mood swing, no lawyer in a fancy hat. The lender lets it go because the LORD called the time. I've been left in a drawer for years and never once got a notice that nice. Release means release, friend.

explanations.answer: The neighbor has already paid it back twice
explanations.explanation: Paid back twice? Friend, I'd love to meet that neighbor. The text never says anything about the debt being paid at all. The lender stops collecting because the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed (Deuteronomy 15:2).

explanations.answer: The elders at the city gate have voided it
explanations.explanation: That sounds official, with a stamp and a long line, but the text never mentions elders in this verse. The reason it gives is that the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed. The release comes from the LORD, not from a ruling at the gate.

I see why you'd say that, but verse 3 draws a line. It says, “You may collect something from a foreigner, but you must forgive whatever your brother owes you.” So the release covers what a brother owes. A foreigner's debt isn't wiped out by it.

Yes, baker, it's false. Verse 3 says, “You may collect something from a foreigner, but you must forgive whatever your brother owes you.” The release is for the debts of a brother. A foreigner's debt isn't covered by it.

That's right. Moses says the blessing comes “…if only you obey the LORD your God and are careful to follow all these commandments I am giving you today.” Notice the words "if only." The promise and the obeying are tied together in the same breath.

It does come with a condition. Verse 5 says the blessing comes “…if only you obey the LORD your God and are careful to follow all these commandments I am giving you today.” The promise in verse 4 and the obeying in verse 5 are joined together. I'd read them together, friend.
Yes, baker. Verse 6 says, “…you will lend to many nations but borrow from none…” Israel would be the one with money to lend, not the one asking. That's the LORD's blessing in action.
Right again. The verse says, “you will rule over many nations but be ruled by none.” That's the second half of the blessing. Israel would be the one holding the reins.

Owing is a fair guess, because borrowing and owing go together like dough and an oven. But the blank wants the word that matches the first half of the promise. Verse 6 says, “…you will lend to many nations but borrow from none…” The word the verse uses is lend, and owe never shows up.

Bow is a fair guess, because people do bow to whoever's in charge. But verse 6 never mentions bowing. It says Israel will “…rule over many nations but be ruled by none.” Rule is the word that fits that blank, baker.

Selling is a fair guess, since money talk shows up all over this passage. But verse 6 doesn't mention selling at all. It says Israel will lend to many nations but borrow from none, and rule over many nations but be ruled by none. Lend and rule are the words that fit the blanks.

explanations.answer: Open his hand and loan what he needs
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Verse 8 says, “Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs.” Think about a fist. You can't hold anything out with a fist, and you can't take anything either. An open hand can do both, and “freely” is the word that does the work.

explanations.answer: Point him to a richer man in town
explanations.explanation: Pointing down the road and wishing him luck would be pretty easy, wouldn't it? But verse 8 puts the open hand on the man who's standing right there. He is to “…freely loan him whatever he needs.” The text gives no instruction to send the poor brother down the road to somebody else.

explanations.answer: Hire him to work for one season
explanations.explanation: Hiring him sounds sensible, but it's not what this verse says. Verse 8 says the Israelite is to “…open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs.” There's no season of work in it. It's an open hand and a free loan.

That's exactly where Moses says it leads. The thought is that the year of release is near, “so that you look upon your poor brother begrudgingly and give him nothing.” Moses calls it a wicked thought. It starts quietly in the heart, and it ends with an empty hand.
Double would be a cold move, but the text doesn't say that. Verse 9 says the wicked thought leads to looking at your poor brother begrudgingly and giving him nothing. It ends with an empty hand.
A field never comes up in this warning, friend. Verse 9 says the wicked thought makes a man look at his poor brother begrudgingly and “…give him nothing.” The danger Moses names is the closed hand.

That's right. Verse 9 says, “He will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.” The poor brother might have no one else to turn to, but he can cry out to the LORD. Moses takes that seriously, and so should we.
It's true, baker. Verse 9 says, “He will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.” That's what Moses warns about the man who gives his brother nothing. It's a serious line.

You got it, baker. Moses says the LORD “…will bless you in all your work and in everything to which you put your hand.” The giving is meant to be free and without a grieving heart. And the blessing covers the whole of a man's work, not just one corner of it.

Testing is a reasonable guess, since this passage has plenty of hard commands. But verse 10 doesn't say "test." It says the LORD “…will bless you in all your work and in everything to which you put your hand.” The generous giver hears about blessing.

I get why judging came to mind, since verse 9 had a warning in it. But verse 10 is about the one who gives generously without a grieving heart. For him, Moses says the LORD “…will bless you in all your work and in everything to which you put your hand.” That's a promise, not a verdict.
That's right. Verse 12 says, “…in the seventh year you must set him free.” Six years of serving, then the door opens. And notice the word must, because the master doesn't get to decide otherwise.
Selling is how this servant came into the household, since verse 12 says he was "…sold to you…" But it's not how the seventh year goes. In that year the master must set him free.

Keeping him would be easy for the master, since the work is already getting done. But verse 12 says it plainly: “…in the seventh year you must set him free.” After six years, the servant goes free. Keeping him isn't the master's call.

explanations.answer: As the LORD has blessed him
explanations.explanation: That's the measure, baker. Verse 14 says, “You shall give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you.” The master gives from his flock, his threshing floor and his winepress. The size of the gift follows the size of his blessing.

That would put the servant in charge of the number, but the verse doesn't say so. It says the master is to “…give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you.” The measure is what the LORD has given the master.

explanations.answer: One tenth of that year's harvest
explanations.explanation: A tenth sounds like a tidy number, but verse 14 doesn't name a fraction. It says, “You shall give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you.” The master gives from his flock, his threshing floor and his winepress. The measure is his own blessing, not a set percentage.

explanations.answer: They were slaves in Egypt and the LORD redeemed them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Moses gives. Verse 15 says, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today.” Israel knows from its own history what it was to be slaves and to be redeemed. Moses points them back to that when he gives the command about their servants.

explanations.answer: Freed servants will speak well of their old masters
explanations.explanation: It would be nice to get a good review from a freed servant, but that's not the reason in the text. Verse 15 says, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you…” The reason is something Israel remembers about themselves.

explanations.answer: The nations around them are watching how they live
explanations.explanation: Nothing in verse 15 mentions the nations watching. Moses is the one speaking here, and he says, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today.” The reason isn't about who might be looking. It's about what Israel remembers about itself.

explanations.answer: He loves his master and household and is well off
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Verse 16 says he says it “because he loves you and your household and is well off with you…” He isn't stuck, since the door is open and he chooses to stay. That's a good household to be in.

explanations.answer: He has no family left to go home to
explanations.explanation: That would be a sad reason, and the text doesn't give it. Verse 16 says the servant stays “because he loves you and your household and is well off with you…” It tells us about love and being well off. It doesn't tell us about missing family.

explanations.answer: He still owes his master money from a loan
explanations.explanation: A loan sounds like it fits, since this passage started with loans. But verse 16 says nothing about a debt. The servant stays “because he loves you and your household and is well off with you…”

explanations.answer: For the rest of his life
explanations.explanation: That's right. Verse 17 says that after the awl goes through his ear into the door, “…he will become your servant for life.” He chose it with the door open. Once he chooses, it's for life.
Six more years has a nice ring, since it's the length of the first stretch. But verse 17 says he “…will become your servant for life.” It doesn't put a new time limit on it.

explanations.answer: Until the next year of release
explanations.explanation: That would make the seventh year a revolving door. But verse 17 says the servant who chooses to stay “…will become your servant for life.” He stays for life, with no countdown to another release.

I get why you'd think so, but verse 17 closes that door. After telling about the manservant, Moses says, “And treat your maidservant the same way.” So she's treated the same way. The text doesn't split them.
Yes, baker. Verse 17 ends with this line: “And treat your maidservant the same way.” Moses names the maidservant on purpose. She's treated the same way as the manservant.

You got it, baker. Verse 18 says the servant's “…six years of service were worth twice the wages of a hired hand.” So when a master frees his servant, Moses says he shouldn't regard it as a hardship. He got twice the value, and the LORD will bless him in all he does.

Half would make freeing a servant feel like a loss, but the text says the opposite. Verse 18 says his six years were worth “…twice the wages of a hired hand.” That's why Moses tells the master not to treat it as a hardship.
A tenth would be a pretty small return on six years, friend. But verse 18 says the servant's six years were worth “…twice the wages of a hired hand.” Twice, not a tenth.

That's right, baker. Verse 19 says, “You must set apart to the LORD your God every firstborn male produced by your herds and flocks.” Every one of them. The verse goes on to say the firstborn of the oxen aren't to be put to work, and the firstborn of the flock aren't to be sheared. Not a bad deal for an ox, while I'm over here stamping cookies all day.
It's true, baker. Verse 19 says, “You must set apart to the LORD your God every firstborn male produced by your herds and flocks.” The word every is right there. Moses isn't picking and choosing.
